feed.title: ME/CFS Research Watch
feed.subtitle: New ME/CFS drug trials in Germany and notable new research papers.

entry.title: Paper: DNA methylation: unifying framework for complex chronic conditions
entry.summary:
This review looks at DNA methylation, chemical tags that switch genes on or off, in ME/CFS, long COVID, fibromyalgia and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. These conditions share many symptoms, and the authors think they may share a biological root.
Why it matters: The authors argue for studying these conditions together, which could lead to shared biomarkers and treatment targets.
Trends in Genetics · Sharma, Rodger, Chatterjee, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tig.2026.09.001

entry.title: Paper: Shared Clinical and Immunological Features of Post-Acute COVID-19 and Post-Acute COVID-19 Vaccination Syndromes
entry.summary:
A German team compared people with lasting fatigue and other symptoms after a COVID-19 infection with people whose similar symptoms began after a COVID-19 vaccination. Both groups had similar autoantibodies against stress-hormone and nerve receptors. Many still had spike protein, a piece of the virus or vaccine, in their blood, especially those whose symptoms began after vaccination.
Why it matters: Fatigue illness after infection and after vaccination seems to share the same immune problem. Leftover spike protein together with self-attacking antibodies may drive the illness, whatever the trigger was.
medRxiv (preprint, not yet peer-reviewed) · Dinser J, Anft M, Wiemers L, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.18.26363380

entry.title: Paper: Chronic Stress Primes TLR3-Mediated Systemic Inflammation to Produce Persistent Post-Viral Fatigue Syndrome-Like Symptoms in Mice
entry.summary:
Mice that were stressed for a long time and then given a molecule that mimics a viral infection developed lasting fatigue, pain sensitivity, memory problems and less social behaviour, similar to post-viral fatigue syndrome. Minocycline, a drug that calms overactive immune cells in the brain, partly reversed these effects.
Why it matters: In a controlled animal model, stress followed by a virus-like immune trigger caused lasting ME/CFS-like symptoms through brain inflammation, and calming that inflammation partly undid them. This supports brain inflammation as a treatable driver of post-viral fatigue.
Neuroscience · Lkhagvasuren B, Suematsu T, Xiangyu L, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroscience.2026.07.002

entry.title: Paper: Regulatory Cycles of Orexin and Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 in Postviral Syndromes
entry.summary:
Orexin is a brain messenger that keeps us awake and helps regulate energy use, sleep and hormones. This review argues that faulty orexin signalling, together with changes in the gut-brain hormone GLP-1, may help explain the exhaustion, sleep problems and metabolic changes in long COVID and ME/CFS.
Why it matters: Both hormone systems already have approved drugs: orexin-targeting medicines and GLP-1 drugs used for diabetes and weight loss. They could be starting points for treating the underlying biology of ME/CFS and long COVID.
Endocrine Reviews · Ruhrländer J, Schieffer E, Schieffer B https://doi.org/10.1210/endrev/bnag009

entry.title: Paper: Can Depression Polygenic Risk Score Predict Postinfective Fatigue Syndrome (PIFS) in the Dubbo Infection Outcomes Study (DIOS)?
entry.summary:
Researchers followed 464 people after a confirmed infection such as glandular fever to see who developed postinfective fatigue syndrome, a CFS-like illness, six months later. They tested whether inherited genetic risk for depression or for chronic fatigue syndrome predicted who became ill.
Why it matters: Neither genetic risk score predicted the illness. That argues against the idea that post-infective ME/CFS-like illness is hidden depression. A weak hint that depression risk genes raise the odds in women and lower them in men needs a larger study.
Twin Research and Human Genetics · Ruseva AG, Valencia BM, Gordon SD, et al. https://doi.org/10.1017/thg.2026.10098

entry.title: Paper: Evaluation of an Integrated Multidisciplinary Care Model for Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Prospective, Open-label, Non-randomized Controlled Intervention Study
entry.summary:
The Charité Fatigue Centrum tested a structured care programme for ME/CFS against usual care with a single visit. The programme included pacing advice, sleep and pain management, nutrition advice, social support and tailored inpatient rehabilitation. 89 patients were in the programme and 93 had usual care, each followed for a year.
Why it matters: The extra care did not improve physical function or other key outcomes after a year, and disability got worse in almost half of the programme group. Better-organised care alone does not replace an effective medical treatment.
The American Journal of Medicine · Peters CK (formerly published as Kedor C), Mödl L, Rust R, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amjmed.2026.09.013

entry.title: Paper: Hemodynamic Phenotyping in ME/CFS and ANOCA: Complementary Insights from Coronary Function Testing and Invasive Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing
entry.summary:
261 people with unexplained chest pain had detailed heart and blood-vessel tests. 18% of them also had ME/CFS, and 89% of these had ANOCA, a condition where the heart's smallest vessels do not work properly although the main arteries look normal. During exercise their hearts delivered oxygen normally, but their muscles had trouble using it, which points to a problem in the muscle.
Why it matters: Finding this small-vessel problem changed treatment for 81% of the affected patients. Some chest pain and exercise intolerance in ME/CFS may fit a known, testable heart condition.
American Journal of Physiology-Heart and Circulatory Physiology · Mackay Z, Shah S, Villalobos JG, et al. https://doi.org/10.1152/ajpheart.90080.2026

entry.title: Paper: Clinical Symptomatology, Cognition and Psychosocial Wellbeing in Adolescents With Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Cross-Sectional Observational Study
entry.summary:
Researchers in Melbourne compared 25 teenagers with mild to moderate ME/CFS with 25 healthy teenagers. Overall intelligence was normal in the ME/CFS group, but they processed information measurably more slowly. They also reported much worse sleep and quality of life and more anxiety and depression. Parents noticed problems with attention and memory.
Why it matters: The brain fog young patients describe is a real, measurable slowing of processing speed, not lower intelligence. That supports flexible arrangements at school instead of telling teenagers to try harder.
Journal of Paediatrics and Child Health · Chau T, Josev EK, Scheinberg A, et al. https://doi.org/10.1111/jpc.70587

entry.title: Paper: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome and overlapping post-acute infection syndromes: international expert consensus framework for diagnostic standardization
entry.summary:
19 international ME/CFS experts agreed on a standard way to measure and score seven core symptoms of ME/CFS and related post-infection illnesses, including long COVID. Among them are post-exertional malaise, problems with automatic body functions such as heart rate or blood pressure, brain fog and sleep problems. They also set out a stepwise testing plan that avoids unnecessary or risky tests.
Why it matters: A shared way of measuring symptoms makes studies and drug trials from different centres easier to compare.
BMC Medicine · Kujawski S, Eaton-Fitch N, Słomko J, et al. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-026-05161-8

entry.title: Paper: A systems microbiology framework for reproducible multi-dataset omics integration with application to long COVID
entry.summary:
Researchers built a new computer method to combine several small, inconsistent gene-activity studies of long COVID. They found seven genes for immune response and energy production that showed up across different patient groups, and matched them to existing drugs that might be repurposed.
Why it matters: A short list of targets and approved drugs to look at for long COVID, and a method that could find similar signals in ME/CFS.
Frontiers in Systems Biology · Varga B, Martinez-Archundia M, Willemsen LEM, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fsysb.2026.1873899

entry.title: Paper: Voluntary wheel running behavior is reduced by SARS-CoV-2 S1 administration and mitigates hypothalamic neuroinflammatory processes
entry.summary:
In rats, injecting part of the coronavirus spike protein into the brain fluid made the animals run less on their own, which researchers use as a sign of fatigue. Letting the rats run voluntarily reduced the brain inflammation the spike protein had caused.
Why it matters: An animal model linking a virus protein to brain inflammation and less activity. In this model some exercise calmed the inflammation, which contrasts with reports that exertion harms people with ME/CFS.
Brain, Behavior, & Immunity - Health · Kelley T, Frank MG, Ball JB, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbih.2026.101331

entry.title: Paper: Gut microbiome signatures during acute infection are associated with long COVID
entry.summary:
People were followed from their first COVID-19 infection onwards. The mix of gut bacteria during the acute illness, not later, predicted who would develop long COVID. Different bacterial patterns went with different symptom patterns.
Why it matters: A gut-bacteria test during the first infection might one day show who is at risk of long COVID. The link between gut and immune system could be an early treatment target.
Gut Microbes · Comba IY, Mars RAT, Yang L, et al. https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2026.2718581

entry.title: Paper: The Post-COVID syndrome caused by excessive inflammation: pathogenesis, potential targets and therapeutic agents
entry.summary:
A review of the evidence that ongoing, excessive inflammation drives long-COVID fatigue, with a list of drugs and other treatments being explored to calm it.
Why it matters: A list of anti-inflammatory drug candidates that future long-COVID and ME/CFS trials could test.
Frontiers in Pharmacology · Zhou T, Xue G, Zhang Y, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fphar.2026.1852220

entry.title: Paper: Subclinical neurovascular and immune correlates of post-COVID-19 syndrome detected by retinal imaging
entry.summary:
Detailed eye imaging found small changes in the tiny blood vessels and in immune activity at the back of the eye in people with post-COVID syndrome, even when standard eye exams were normal.
Why it matters: The retina is one of the few places where doctors can look directly at small vessels and nerve tissue. These changes give a non-invasive view of vessel and immune problems that may underlie fatigue after COVID and in ME/CFS.
Brain, Behavior, & Immunity - Health · Wunderle M, Wicklein R, Ribeiro A, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbih.2026.101315

entry.title: Paper: Effect of low-dose naltrexone for long COVID: a systematic review and meta-analysis
entry.summary:
This review pooled the available studies on low-dose naltrexone (LDN), a cheap generic drug that many people with long COVID and ME/CFS use off-label, to see whether it helps with symptoms such as fatigue.
Why it matters: LDN is one of the treatments patients try most often. An independent review of the evidence helps decide whether it deserves a proper clinical trial.
BMJ Open · Byambasuren O, Atkins T, Baptista S, et al. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-111253

entry.title: Paper: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome in adolescents with ME/CFS — a case control study
entry.summary:
Doctors gave 18 teenagers with ME/CFS and 18 healthy teenagers a simple 10-minute standing test that records heart rate and blood pressure. More than a third of the ME/CFS group had postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), where the heart races too much on standing. None of the healthy teens did. The rise in heart rate during the test alone found POTS almost as well as a specialist examination.
Why it matters: A simple, cheap test that any doctor could use to find a treatable circulation problem in teenagers with ME/CFS, which could speed up diagnosis and treatment.
Frontiers in Pediatrics · Leone A, Gerrer K, Viereck A, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fped.2026.1836407

entry.title: Paper: Seven replicated genomic associations of myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: a biobank study
entry.summary:
Researchers used genetic data from the UK Biobank (about 1,268 people with ME/CFS) and checked the results in two smaller groups. Seven gene regions came up again and again. In one of them (CLYBL), the variant linked to ME/CFS goes with lower activity of that gene in brain tissue.
Why it matters: The same gene hits now show up outside DecodeME as well. That makes a genetic basis for ME/CFS more likely and gives drug researchers specific genes to look at.
medRxiv (preprint) · Slaughter J, Labayle O, Roskams-Hieter B, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.09.26362115

entry.title: Paper: Clinical Phenotypes of Post-Acute Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC) Infection: A Longitudinal Cohort Study from Karachi, Pakistan
entry.summary:
A year-long study in Karachi, Pakistan, followed long-COVID patients' symptoms together with virus remnants in stool samples and serotonin levels in the blood. Most symptoms eased over time, but muscle pain, weakness and fatigue lasted in many. People who still had virus in their stool more often reported breathlessness, fatigue, weakness and joint pain.
Why it matters: Rare long-term data from South Asia. It supports two mechanisms proposed for ME/CFS-like fatigue: leftover virus in the gut and disturbed serotonin signalling.
medRxiv (preprint) · Khanum I, Ahmed K, Munir T, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.04.26361413

entry.title: Paper: Total blood volume and red blood cell volume are not associated with orthostatic intolerance in adults with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome
entry.summary:
Researchers measured the actual volume of blood and red blood cells in 49 adults with ME/CFS and then tested how they reacted to standing up. More than half had an abnormal standing test, with dizziness, a racing heart or changes in breathing. Whether their blood volume was low, normal or high made no difference.
Why it matters: Low blood volume has long been suspected as the cause of standing intolerance in ME/CFS. This study suggests it is not the main cause. Nerves, blood vessels, breathing or brain blood flow look like better treatment targets.
Physiological Reports · Yamazaki T, Mancini DM, Blate M, et al. https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.71087

entry.title: Paper: Exercise Lactate in Post-COVID-19 Condition: Pathophysiological Signal, Phenotyping Tool, or Candidate Biomarker? A Narrative Review with a Hypothesis-Generating Clinical Observation
entry.summary:
This review looks at lactate measured during exercise in people with long COVID. Muscles make lactate when they cannot produce energy efficiently. The authors add a small case series of 22 patients whose lactate at peak effort was about six times higher than at rest. They conclude that lactate varies too much between people and test methods to diagnose the condition on its own.
Why it matters: Post-exertional malaise is hard to measure objectively. Exercise lactate is an early candidate marker for poor energy metabolism, but the review says it is not ready for clinical use.
Current Problems in Cardiology · Sakellaropoulos SG, Spedicato V, Pfister O https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpcardiol.2026.103453

entry.title: Paper: Mapping the complexity of ME/CFS: Evidence for abnormal energy metabolism, altered immune profile, and vascular dysfunction
entry.summary:
Comparing blood from ME/CFS patients and healthy people, researchers found several problems at once. Immune cells were short of ATP, the cell's fuel. Several types of immune cells looked less mature than normal. Blood proteins linked to clotting and blood-vessel reactions were raised, a sign that the vessel lining is not working well.
Why it matters: One study that shows energy, immune and blood-vessel problems together in ME/CFS. These markers could help with diagnosis or serve as treatment targets.
Cell Reports Medicine · Heng B, Gunasegaran B, Krishnamurthy S, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xcrm.2025.102514

entry.title: Paper: Fatigue is associated with stimulus-related theta and alpha power and distinguishes subjective from objective cognition in a post-viral cohort: A cross-sectional study
entry.summary:
In a large German group of people after viral infections, EEG recordings showed that those who felt more fatigued had different brain-wave patterns (theta and alpha waves) during mental tasks, even when their test results looked normal.
Why it matters: An objective marker for a common and puzzling gap in ME/CFS and long COVID: people feel very fatigued although their test performance looks normal.
Research Square (preprint) · Neumann C, Godbersen L, Schmeer L, et al. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10753262/v1

entry.title: Paper: A distinct effector B cell population drives autoantibody production in SARS-CoV-2 infection
entry.summary:
In blood from COVID-19 patients, researchers found a specific kind of B cell that makes autoantibodies, which attack the body's own tissue. They also identified the signal that switches these cells on.
Why it matters: Autoantibodies are a main suspect in ME/CFS and long COVID. Knowing which cells make them and what turns them on gives drug developers a precise target.
Immunity · Yuan D, Li S, Zhang R, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.immuni.2026.08.002

entry.title: Paper: Cognition-Linked Monocyte State Reveals Altered Myeloid-Lymphoid Coordination in Neuro-PASC
entry.summary:
In older adults with long-COVID brain fog, researchers found certain white blood cells (monocytes) in an unusual state, together with poorer coordination between different parts of the immune system.
Why it matters: Faulty immune cells, not only direct brain damage, may be behind fatigue and thinking problems in long COVID and ME/CFS.
International Journal of Molecular Sciences · Hanson BA, Cogswell AC, Lopez M, et al. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27167474

entry.title: Paper: Loss of vesicular monoamine transporter 2 in striatum of long COVID and relationship to neuropsychiatric symptoms
entry.summary:
Brain scans of people with long COVID showed fewer working dopamine-releasing nerve endings in a region for motivation and movement. The bigger the loss, the more apathetic, slowed down or forgetful people felt.
Why it matters: A measurable brain change behind some motivation and thinking problems in long COVID. Treatments that boost dopamine signalling could be tested.
EBioMedicine · Liu YK, Persaud D, Vieira EL, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106339

entry.title: Paper: Acute Protein Responses Control SARS-CoV-2-specific Neurocognitive and General Post-Viral Sequelae
entry.summary:
Saliva samples were taken soon after a COVID-19 infection. People who made more of certain antiviral immune proteins early on were less likely to have lasting brain fog and fatigue months later.
Why it matters: A simple early saliva test might one day show who is at risk of long-term post-viral fatigue. The proteins could also be treatment targets.
medRxiv (preprint) · Liou TG, Andrews RJ, Bass BL, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.27.26361488

entry.title: Paper: Abnormal post-exercise depression of corticomotor excitability is associated with fatigue in post-COVID-19 condition
entry.summary:
Researchers used magnetic pulses to test the signal from brain to muscle before and after exercise in 58 people with long COVID. The brain's motor output did not recover normally after effort, and this matched how tired patients said they felt.
Why it matters: An objective, brain-based way to measure fatigue after exertion, instead of relying only on how tired people say they are. It could help with diagnosis and in trials.
Clinical Neurophysiology · Sebastianelli L, Dezi S, Ortelli P, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clinph.2026.2112384

entry.title: Paper: Beyond genes: EpiSwitch® and Orion platform-powered 3D genome architecture biomarkers reveal shared biology across ME/CFS, long COVID, PTSD, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis
entry.summary:
Some genes are switched on or off by how DNA is folded inside the cell, not only by the DNA code. Using a method that reads this folding, researchers compared blood from people with ME/CFS, long COVID, PTSD, rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis. They found folding patterns that these very different illnesses share.
Why it matters: These conditions may share some measurable biology. The work extends the same group's earlier ME/CFS blood test (EpiSwitch) to a comparison across diseases that could later help with diagnosis.
Journal of Translational Medicine · Hunter E, Alshaker H, Vugrinec D, et al. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12967-026-08874-9

entry.title: Paper: Uncovering the hidden biology of fibrinaloid microclot complexes in complex, inflammatory diseases
entry.summary:
Microclots are unusually tough blood clots that are hard to dissolve. Some researchers think they build up in inflammatory illnesses. This review from a leading microclot group explains how they form, why the body has trouble breaking them down and how they might cause symptoms in ME/CFS and long COVID.
Why it matters: From Etheresia Pretorius and Douglas Kell, the group best known for this work. It summarises and extends the microclot and blood-vessel theory behind some treatment ideas in ME/CFS and long COVID.
QRB Discovery · Grixti J, Pretorius E, Kell DB https://doi.org/10.1017/qrd.2026.10022

entry.title: Paper: Small extracellular vesicles proteome reveals persistent inflammatory and coagulopathic dysregulation in long-COVID
entry.summary:
In long-COVID patients with fatigue, brain fog and sleep problems, the proteins carried by tiny blood particles (extracellular vesicles) showed lasting signs of inflammation and abnormal clotting.
Why it matters: Another lab with another method finds inflammation and abnormal clotting in long COVID, the same area as the microclot research.
Frontiers in Immunology · Chandran S, Chen L, Ram AK, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1805159

entry.title: Paper: Associations between multidimensional fatigue and wearable-derived cardio-respiratory variables in post-COVID-19 patients: an observational study
entry.summary:
30 people in post-COVID rehabilitation wore sensors day and night that recorded heart rate and breathing. Physical, mental and emotional tiredness each matched a different pattern in these signals.
Why it matters: Wrist or chest sensors could track different kinds of fatigue over time. That helps with pacing and with measuring whether treatments work.
Frontiers in Digital Health · Adão Martins NR, Annaheim S, Büche D, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdgth.2026.1804993

entry.title: Paper: Symptom-based clusters in people with post-COVID-19 condition (PCC)
entry.summary:
In 1,673 people with post-COVID condition in Germany, researchers grouped patients by their pattern of 14 symptoms, including fatigue, instead of using one label. They found distinct subgroups that differed in age, sex and psychological factors.
Why it matters: A large German study showing that post-COVID condition is not one illness but several subgroups. That matters for tailoring treatment and for who German trials include.
Journal of Translational Medicine · Kuczyk C, Herrmann-Lingen C, Stolz M, et al. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12967-026-08582-4

entry.title: Paper: Low serum selenium combined with SELENOP-autoantibodies are associated with persistent fatigue after SARS-CoV-2 infection
entry.summary:
Selenium is a mineral the body needs, and SELENOP is the blood protein that carries it. In about 750 adults roughly two years after COVID-19, people with low selenium and antibodies against SELENOP were more likely to still have fatigue. A selenium shortage, possibly made worse by the immune system attacking its carrier, may add to lasting tiredness.
Why it matters: Selenium plus SELENOP antibodies is an easy-to-measure marker for post-viral fatigue. Whether selenium supplements help could be tested in a trial.
Redox Biology · Schmidt B, Asaad S, Mavarani L, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.redox.2026.104273

entry.title: Paper: Molecular, cellular and network mapping of brain structural deviations in patients with Post-COVID19 syndrome
entry.summary:
Brain scans of 20 people with lasting tiredness after a mild COVID-19 infection showed small changes in thickness in certain brain regions. These were mainly regions rich in the protein the coronavirus uses to enter cells, and regions involved in mood and the messenger serotonin.
Why it matters: Brain scans show that fatigue can follow even a mild infection and link it to specific biology, such as virus entry points and serotonin circuits, that could become drug targets.
Brain, Behavior, & Immunity - Health · Martins D, Cai Z, Mariani N, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bbih.2026.101292

entry.title: Paper: Increased Mannosylation of Extracellular Vesicles in Long COVID Plasma as a Binding Target for Galanthus nivalis Agglutinin (GNA) Affinity Resin
entry.summary:
Cells release tiny particles into the blood called extracellular vesicles (EVs). In people with long COVID these particles carry unusual sugar coatings. The researchers showed that a sugar-binding material from a plant can pull these coated particles out of blood. That could lead to a diagnostic test and to a way of filtering them from the blood.
Why it matters: From the well-known LIINC long-COVID group at UCSF. A new biomarker idea and a possible blood-filtering treatment, similar in principle to immunoadsorption.
International Journal of Molecular Sciences · Pesqueira Sanchez MA, de Necochea Campion R, Dalhuisen T, et al. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27135723

entry.title: Paper: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome in Long COVID: prevalence and impact on health-related quality of life and health status. A cross-sectional study. BioICOPER study
entry.summary:
Among 304 people with long COVID in Spain, a sizeable group met older formal criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome. This group had clearly worse quality of life and general health than the other long-COVID patients.
Why it matters: It shows how large and how badly affected the ME/CFS-like group within long COVID is, which matters for how these patients are defined, studied and prioritised.
Research Square (preprint) · Navarro-Cáceres A, Gómez-Sánchez L, Suárez-Moreno N, et al. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-9593874/v1

entry.title: Paper: Pilot longitudinal integrated transcriptomic-metabolomic study reveals immune and metabolic signatures in non-hospitalized healthcare workers with long COVID
entry.summary:
Healthcare workers who developed long COVID after a mild infection, with fatigue and brain fog as main symptoms, had unusual patterns in their immune-cell genes and blood chemistry compared with colleagues who fully recovered.
Why it matters: Most biomarker studies look at people who were in hospital. This one looks at the milder, more ME/CFS-like form that is harder to study but affects many more people.
Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology · Espín E, Yang C, Shannon CP, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fcimb.2026.1808564

entry.title: Paper: Prevalence and Functional Outcomes of Post-Exertional Malaise among Adults with prior COVID-19: Results from a Representative Survey of New York City Residents
entry.summary:
A survey of more than 9,600 adults in New York City who had had COVID-19 found that about one in five still has post-exertional malaise (PEM), a crash after physical or mental effort. Around 4% have symptoms that have lasted long enough to meet ME/CFS criteria.
Why it matters: One of the largest representative estimates of how common PEM is after COVID-19. Women, trans and non-binary people, people of colour, and people with less education or existing disabilities are hit hardest. Doctors should routinely ask about PEM.
medRxiv (preprint) · Packard SE, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.31.26356614

entry.title: Paper: Micronutrition as a Therapeutic Strategy for Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome and Fibromyalgia: A Narrative Review
entry.summary:
This review sums up evidence that faulty energy production in the cells (mitochondrial dysfunction) and damage from unstable molecules (oxidative stress) contribute to ME/CFS and fibromyalgia. It asks whether nutrients such as NAD+ precursors, B vitamins, magnesium and CoQ10 could help.
Why it matters: A plausible, low-risk approach, but the authors say there is little trial evidence for these supplements in ME/CFS so far and call for proper randomised trials.
Nutrients · Abanades S, Fernandez I, Capdevila N, et al. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu18162702

entry.title: Paper: Auditory sensory gating (P50 suppression) as a biomarker of cognitive fatigue in long COVID
entry.summary:
Researchers measured a brain-wave response called P50 suppression, which shows how well the brain filters out repeated, unimportant sounds, in 71 people with long-COVID fatigue. The worse the filtering, the more mental fatigue people reported, even after taking depression into account.
Why it matters: A simple, objective brain-wave measure that tracks mental fatigue independently of mood. It could help build a test for brain fog in long COVID and ME/CFS.
Neuropsychology · Mischke M, Zaehle T https://doi.org/10.1037/neu0001120

entry.title: Paper: Nutraceuticals targeting mitochondrial and oxidative-inflammatory pathways for post-exertional malaise and cognitive impairment in long COVID: a narrative review
entry.summary:
This review collects research on cellular energy production (mitochondria), harmful oxygen by-products (oxidative stress) and inflammatory signals. It proposes that certain vitamins, minerals and supplements acting on these pathways could help with crashes after exertion and brain fog in long COVID. None of this has been tested as a treatment.
Why it matters: A plan for future supplement trials in long COVID and ME/CFS. It is a review without new patient data, so it does not show that any supplement works.
Nutrients · Praet SFE https://doi.org/10.3390/nu18162650

entry.title: Paper: Fragile mitophagy and post-exertional malaise in long COVID: a hypothesis
entry.summary:
This paper suggests a new reason why people with long COVID crash one to three days after activity. Damaged mitochondria are marked for clean-up, but the clean-up is not finished. Leftover debris from the mitochondria then keeps inflammation going long after the activity.
Why it matters: A new idea for explaining PEM that could be tested with existing lab methods. It is a single author's hypothesis without new data.
Frontiers in Medicine · Groysman R https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1905758

entry.title: Paper: Nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for the treatment of long COVID (RECOVER-VITAL): a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial
entry.summary:
In this large US trial, 959 adults who had had long-COVID symptoms for at least 12 weeks were randomly given the antiviral Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) or a placebo for 15 or 25 days. The aim was to test whether hidden virus drives the symptoms. The drug was no better than placebo on any measure, whether people mainly had brain fog, dizziness and a fast heart rate, or exercise intolerance.
Why it matters: The largest and most careful test so far of the idea that leftover virus causes long COVID. It found no benefit. Research now turns to other explanations, including for the form with crashes after exertion that overlaps with ME/CFS.
The Lancet Infectious Diseases · Baden LR, Shah NS, Liu STH, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/S1473-3099(26)00406-8

entry.title: Paper: Cognitive rehabilitation for adults with long COVID: a randomized clinical trial
entry.summary:
In a trial in England, 78 adults with lasting brain fog after COVID-19 were randomly assigned to ten weekly one-to-one sessions of cognitive rehabilitation or to usual care. The sessions were practical coaching on everyday goals they chose themselves, such as remembering appointments. The coaching group made clearly more progress on their goals, and much of the benefit lasted six months.
Why it matters: A well-designed randomised trial showing that a non-drug treatment can help with long-COVID brain fog, for which there is no approved treatment.
JAMA Network Open · Vanova M, Patel AMR, Scott I, et al. https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.20687

entry.title: Paper: Wearable-derived cardiopulmonary fitness and physical activity in adults with long COVID: a RECOVER-Adult digital health substudy
entry.summary:
Almost 1,500 people wore fitness trackers about 21 months after COVID-19. Those with many long-COVID symptoms had lower heart-rate variability at rest, a faster resting pulse and were much less active day to day than those with few symptoms.
Why it matters: Wearable data, not just questionnaires, show a lasting drop in heart and activity fitness almost two years after infection. Whether long COVID becomes a long-term risk for heart health is an open question.
JACC: Advances · Vogel JM, Jenkins T, Cerda M, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacadv.2026.102923

entry.title: Paper: A comparative analysis of computational clustering methods for symptom-based classification of long COVID
entry.summary:
Patient researchers analysed answers from more than 6,000 people with long COVID about 162 symptoms and used three different computer methods to sort them into subtypes. The methods mostly disagreed about which subtypes exist, so long-COVID symptoms look more like a spectrum than clear categories. People with more symptoms overall always had worse post-exertional malaise and were more often women.
Why it matters: A warning for research on subtypes in long COVID and ME/CFS: which subtype a patient lands in may depend on the statistical method more than on real biology. Trials that select subgroups need to keep this in mind.
Oxford Open Immunology · Green TD, McWilliams C, de Figueiredo L, et al. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfimm/iqag010

entry.title: Paper: Registered interventional trials fail to cover patient-prioritised treatments in Post-COVID condition (PCC)
entry.summary:
Researchers compared 714 registered post-COVID studies (ClinicalTrials.gov, the German DRKS and the EU registry) with 29 treatments that patients and their doctors actually use. Only about 1 in 14 studies tested any of them. 57 trials measured post-exertional malaise (PEM, the crash after activity), but only 8 used it as the main outcome. Ten common types of treatment had no registered trial at all, for example drugs for nervous-system regulation or mast-cell reactions. The German DRKS registry had no trial of any patient-favoured treatment.
Why it matters: Good drug trials that target PEM are rare, and in Germany almost absent. The authors argue that research money, including Germany's new "Nationale Dekade" programme, should also go to the treatments patients and doctors already rely on.
Research Square (preprint) · Gabriel M, Koster S, Puta C, et al. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10851936/v1

entry.title: Paper: A Multivariable Plasma Extracellular Vesicle Surface Profile Associated with Post-COVID-19 Syndrome
entry.summary:
The team studied blood and spinal fluid from 61 people with lasting post-COVID symptoms, 80 people who had fully recovered and 10 people with fatigue after other infections. They looked at the proteins on extracellular vesicles (EVs), tiny particles that cells release into the blood. No single protein separated the groups. A computer model that combined many small differences did tell patients and recovered people apart fairly well, and this EV score went down again a year later in patients who got better.
Why it matters: This could become a new kind of blood test for post-COVID syndrome. The same Ulm team found no unusual immune activity in these patients' brains, so both results point away from autoimmune brain inflammation as the cause.
medRxiv (preprint) · Erhart DK, Ressin H, Balz LT, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.27.26361498

entry.title: Paper: Plasma Proteomics Identifies a Microtesla Magnetic Therapy Response Signature in Long COVID
entry.summary:
In a small trial, people with long-COVID brain fog used a gentle magnetic-field treatment for the whole brain at home ("Microtesla Magnetic Therapy"). Some of them improved. The researchers measured more than 11,000 blood proteins before and after and found about 17 that changed only in the people who got better. One of them normally slows down a signalling pathway (Hedgehog signalling) involved in inflammation and tissue repair, so the treatment may work partly by calming inflammation.
Why it matters: A non-drug treatment produced a measurable change in the blood, and some of these proteins might predict who responds. It is a small feasibility study, so the results are early.
medRxiv (preprint) · Brady NR, Canori A, Maltz D, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.25.26361319

entry.title: Paper: Early HHV-6 IgG and IgA responses during acute SARS-CoV-2 infection in relation to long COVID: a multicohort observational study
entry.summary:
Researchers measured antibodies against HHV-6, a common herpes virus that most people carry in a dormant state, in blood taken when people first caught COVID-19. High IgA antibodies against HHV-6 at that point went with a higher chance of later long COVID. High IgG antibodies went with a lower chance.
Why it matters: A dormant virus becoming active around the time of infection may help set off long COVID or ME/CFS-like illness. It could also lead to an early blood test for people at risk.
EBioMedicine · Choudhury A, Burry MJ Jr, Kwon WJ, et al. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ebiom.2026.106455

entry.title: Paper: VSL#3® supplementation improves fatigue in long COVID: results from the DELong#3 randomized placebo-controlled trial
entry.summary:
In this Italian trial (DELong#3), 48 adults with lasting fatigue after COVID-19 took either a high-dose probiotic with several bacterial strains (VSL#3) or a placebo for four weeks. Fatigue dropped much more with the probiotic, and the improvement was still there a month after they stopped.
Why it matters: One of the few placebo-controlled trials that found less fatigue in long COVID. It points to the gut bacteria as a low-risk treatment target. The trial was small and needs to be repeated with more people.
British Journal of Biomedical Science · Amoroso C, Marinoni B, Maragno P, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/bjbs.2026.16993

entry.title: Paper: eNOS Uncoupling, Shear-Stress Tolerance, and the Two-Threshold Model of Post-Exertional Malaise in Long COVID: A Mechanistic Hypothesis With Implications for Physiotherapy and Recovery Protocols
entry.summary:
This is a theory paper without new patient data. It deals with long-COVID patients who get post-exertional malaise (PEM) even though their blood vessels look normal on standard scans. The authors think COVID-19 damages the inner lining of the vessels and uses up a helper molecule needed to make nitric oxide, a gas that lets vessels widen during activity. Without it, the same enzyme makes harmful by-products instead. These would build up during and after exertion and cause the crash.
Why it matters: It is a blood-vessel explanation for PEM that can be tested with blood samples taken before and after exercise. It differs from Klaus Wirth's muscle-calcium theory. The authors also suggest that too much rest could harm vessel function, which matters for pacing advice.
Microcirculation · Karipidis YK, Karipidis KY https://doi.org/10.1111/micc.70082

entry.title: Paper: Acupressure and Qigong in post-infectious fatigue with impaired physical function: a randomized clinical trial
entry.summary:
In this Charité trial (ACUQiG), 235 people with lasting fatigue and reduced physical function after an infection, mostly COVID-19, were split into two groups. One group pressed on specific body points every day for about 18 minutes (acupressure) and did online Qigong, a gentle movement practice, twice a week for 8 weeks. The other group got a self-care leaflet. Physical function, the main outcome, was only slightly better in the acupressure group, and the difference could have been chance. Fatigue improved a little, and that effect was statistically real.
Why it matters: A careful trial from Carmen Scheibenbogen's group at Charité. It missed its main goal, so expectations for this kind of approach should stay modest, even though fatigue improved slightly.
Frontiers in Medicine · Dietzel J, Bauer T, Tissen-Diabaté T, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1872035

entry.title: Paper: Central noradrenergic deficiency in post-infectious chronic fatigue: neurobehavioral correlates
entry.summary:
Researchers at the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) tested spinal fluid from 16 people with ME/CFS, 34 with long COVID, 32 with Parkinson's disease and 40 healthy volunteers. They measured two brain messengers: noradrenaline, which drives alertness and the fight-or-flight response, and dopamine. People with ME/CFS had clearly less noradrenaline activity than healthy people, even less than the long-COVID and Parkinson's groups. Dopamine was normal. Lower noradrenaline went with weaker grip endurance and worse general health, and it was lowest in people with post-exertional malaise (PEM).
Why it matters: The study links a measurable shortage in the brain to muscle fatigue and symptom severity. The authors think making noradrenaline may cost more energy than ME/CFS cells can supply. Boosting noradrenaline signalling could be a drug target.
Brain Communications · Aregawi L, Walitt B, Sullivan P, et al. https://doi.org/10.1093/braincomms/fcag173

entry.title: Paper: Orthostatic Dysfunction and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome: A Close Reciprocal Relationship Beyond Cardiac Preload Failure and Hypoperfusion
entry.summary:
Standing up puts extra strain on the body, and many people with ME/CFS feel worse when upright (orthostatic intolerance). This paper argues that standing does more than strain the heart and vessels. It may also overload muscle cells with calcium, the same process Klaus Wirth believes causes post-exertional malaise.
Why it matters: Wirth's own hypothesis that standing alone could trigger crashes in severely ill patients through the same mechanism as exertion. It links two of the most disabling symptoms and still needs supporting data.
Preprints.org (preprint) · Wirth KJ https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202608.1772.v1

entry.title: Paper: Persistent Hypercoagulability and Further Characterization of Microclot Complexes in Long COVID
entry.summary:
Blood from 20 people with long COVID and 19 healthy people was tested. The patients' blood clotted faster and more firmly than normal (hypercoagulability) and contained more microclots, small clumps of misfolded blood protein that special dyes can stain.
Why it matters: From Etheresia Pretorius's group, the lab best known for this work. More detailed support for the microclot theory: hard-to-dissolve clots may block small vessels and starve tissue of oxygen.
medRxiv (preprint) · Nunes M, Pereira Guerreiro CM, Pretorius JH, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.20.26360874

entry.title: Paper: Persistent Mitochondrial and Endothelial Dysfunction in Non-Hospitalized Patients with Long COVID
entry.summary:
32 people with long COVID in Japan were followed for 6 months. Two blood markers, one for stress in the mitochondria and one for damage to the blood-vessel lining, stayed high in patients who did not improve and fell in those who did. 91% of the participants had fatigue as a main symptom.
Why it matters: The authors think the same mitochondrial and blood-vessel problems probably underlie fatigue in ME/CFS. The markers could serve as a simple blood test to see who stays ill.
Frontiers in Medicine · Ono R, Takayama S, Abe M, et al. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1921822

entry.title: Paper: Circulating MicroRNA ratios as diagnostic biomarkers for long COVID with an independent validation cohort
entry.summary:
Researchers at the Medical University of Vienna tested blood from 206 long-COVID patients and 71 healthy people for ratios of microRNAs, tiny genetic messengers linked to mitochondria and blood vessels. Two ratios were reliably lower in patients in two separate groups. Accuracy dropped when the test was checked against outside data.
Why it matters: A step towards an objective blood test for long COVID that might also work for ME/CFS. The authors say it is not accurate enough for clinical use yet.
Communications Medicine · Han E, Lukovic D, Müller-Zlabinger K, et al. https://doi.org/10.1038/s43856-026-01854-6

entry.title: Paper: EBV Reprograms B Cells in an Autoimmune-Like Fashion in Patients with COVID-19
entry.summary:
In COVID-19 patients, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a dormant virus most people carry, can wake up and reprogram the B cells it infects so that they act as if they were attacking the body's own tissue. People with more of these reprogrammed cells had worse lingering symptoms 2 to 3 months later.
Why it matters: EBV has long been suspected in long COVID and ME/CFS. This study shows a specific way a reawakened virus could drive lasting illness.
bioRxiv (preprint) · Chen DG, Yuan D, Su Y, et al. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.08.17.745245

entry.title: Paper: A cardiometabolic perspective on post-exertional malaise in myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) and Long COVID
entry.summary:
This opinion paper argues that post-exertional malaise (PEM), the crash after activity, is not one system flaring up. It is a breakdown in how the heart, blood vessels and metabolism work together in the hours and days after exertion, especially in people who also have obesity or type 2 diabetes.
Why it matters: It suggests studying PEM by following the heart and metabolism together over time after exertion, which could help design better drug trials for PEM.
Cardiovascular Diabetology · Westermeier F, Pretorius E, Untersmayr E, et al. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12933-026-03316-8
